# The Days of Duveen: The Silent Men

How did the millionaires of the nineteen-twenties and thirties come to believe that art was more important than money?

By S. N. Behrman

October 27, 1951

Illustration by Saul Steinberg

Save this story

Save this story

_(This is the last of a series of articles on Lord Duveen. [Read the first part](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1951/09/29/the-days-of-duveen) .)_

All his adult life, Joseph Duveen, the most famous art dealer in history, ran a race with his clients’ mortality.

url_citation.title: The Days of Duveen | The New Yorker
url_citation.content:
Profiles

The Days of Duveen

A legendary art dealer and his clients.
By S. N. Behrman
September 22, 1951
Illustration by Saul Steinberg
Save this story
Save this story
(This is the first of a series of articles on Lord Duveen. Read the last part .)
When Joseph Duveen, the most spectacular art dealer of all time, travelled from one to another of his three galleries, in Paris, New York, and London, his business, including a certain amount of his stock in trade, travelled with him. His business was highly personal, and during his absence his establishments dozed.
